title: The Fisherman and His Wife
lines: Once upon a time there was a fisherman and his wife.
They lived in a little hut by the sea,
and they were very poor, for some days a fish took the hook and some days none did.
Well, what happened one day?
What happened was that a terribly big shark got caught on the fisherman's hook.
The fisherman pulled and pulled, but the fish spoke:
"Spare my life! I am not a fish, I am an enchanted prince.
What good would I be to you if you caught me?
You could not eat my flesh anyway."
"You are right," said the fisherman. "Go with God, if you are truly not a real fish."
He let the fish go and went home with an empty bag.
"Well now, did you catch no fish again?"
asked his wife.
"What will become of us?"
"Oh, I did catch one," said the fisherman,
"I caught a terribly big shark, but it was not a real fish.
It said it was an enchanted prince, and it begged until I let it go."
"Well, that was a foolish thing to do.
You should not have let it go until it granted you a wish."
"And what would I have wished for?"
"Why, that it build us a proper house instead of this miserable hut.
Go right back, and if it gets caught on your hook once more,
do not let it go until it promises the house."
The fisherman only shook his head, for he thought it was a useless wish,
but he went back to the seashore and began to call:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
At that very moment the sea gave a great splash,
it sloshed, and up popped the fish and asked the fisherman:
"What do you want, old fisherman?"
The fisherman answered:
"A house is better than a hut.
This is what my wife would like:
A house to live in, not a hut."
Said the fish:
"Go on home, old fisherman,
By morning the house will stand."
And sure enough, by morning a pretty little stone house stood there; they woke in it.
"There, you see," said the wife, "you only have to wish for something and it comes true.
Now go back and tell it that a pretty little stone house
is nice, very nice, but too small for us; it should build a palace instead."
"Oh, wife, wife, what are you thinking?
This house is big enough for us.
What would you do in a palace?"
"Never you mind that, just go and ask for a palace!"
"The fish will be angry, wife, do not be silly!"
"Angry or not, just say what I tell you.
By tomorrow morning there must be a palace here, one as fine as the king's."
What could he do? The fisherman went and called the fish:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
The fish came at once and asked:
"What do you want, old fisherman?"
The fisherman answered:
"That house is too small for us.
This is what my wife would like:
A palace all her own to live in."
Said the fish:
"Then go on home, nice and slow,
In the morning the palace will be ready."
The fisherman went home, they went to bed, and in the morning they woke in a palace,
a palace so huge that it had seventy-seven rooms,
and in the rooms were golden benches, tables, beds, and mirrors down to the floor.
Even the windows were pure gold, and so were the stairs.
Everywhere footmen and maids were bustling about;
not far from the palace stood a great big stable, full of horses with golden coats:
just as the fisherman and his wife stepped inside,
the grooms were combing them with golden combs and brushing them with golden brushes.
"Well," said the wife, "was it not a good thing that I wished for a palace?"
"Good, good," said the fisherman, "now you cannot wish for anything more."
"I will still think about that," said the wife.
The next morning the wife said:
"This palace is fine, very fine, but it would only be truly fine if I were king.
Go to the fish and tell it that I want to be king."
"Wife, wife, what are you saying?
I do not even dare to say that!"
"Why would you not dare?
Just go and tell it boldly that I want to be king."
The fisherman went off very sadly, for he did not like his wife's doings at all.
Now the enchanted prince would surely be angry, and how could he not be!
And indeed, the sea was not clear as at other times, it was grey,
it was dirty, as if it were angry too, and it roared and growled loudly.
But he feared his wife even more than the sea, more
than the enchanted prince, so he called out as before:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me!"
The sea gave a great slosh and splash, the fish popped up and asked the fisherman:
"What is wrong, what is wrong, old fisherman?
Is the house perhaps not big enough?"
The fisherman answered:
"Oh, it is big enough, there is nothing wrong, nothing,
Only my wife wants to be king!"
Said the fish:
"If that is all she wishes for,
Then she shall be king, for sure!"
Well, good Lord, by the time the fisherman got home, the palace had grown bigger,
and the yard too; guards stood in front of the palace,
generals walked up and down in the yard,
the army band played its music, the soldiers marched,
turning right, turning left,
and the fisherman's wife sat in the palace's biggest hall on a throne of pure gold,
guards stood before her, coming and going,
and the people of the court ran about and bowed before her.
"Oh, my Lord!" The fisherman clapped his hands. "So you have really become king?"
"King indeed," said the wife.
"Can you not see?
Here is the crown on my head."
"Well, that is truly a fine thing.
With this you can be content until your dying day."
"You might be content, but not I.
Go back to the fish at once and tell it that I want to be pope."
"Oh wife, wife, what are you saying?
There is only one pope in the whole world, you cannot be that."
"Not another word!" the wife cried out,
"Off with you, or I will have your head cut off at once!"
The poor fisherman shivered all over at this terribly big wish.
But it was no use; still he went to the seashore and spoke to the fish:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
Oh, but the sea was murky, so very murky, and it roared
and rumbled so that the poor fisherman covered his eyes and ears in fright.
Then all at once the fish leapt up, and you could see that it was angry now too.
It shouted at the fisherman:
"Well, what do you want? Come here and tell,
Is being king not enough as well?"
The fisherman answered:
"Oh, it is not enough, not enough,
Now she would like to be pope!"
"Only pope?"
said the shark,
"So be it, let her be pope!"
The fisherman ran home full of joy,
and by the royal palace stood a church so big that its towers (there were a thousand!)
nearly touched the sky. He went in, and there sat his wife on her throne,
kindly giving her blessing to the people, and all who could get near kissed her feet.
So the fisherman pushed his way up too, fell on his knees,
and kissed his wife's feet, and said as he did so:
"Well, wife, now you have become pope as well,
you cannot be more than this, so now you can truly be content."
"We shall see," said the wife.
All night she did not sleep, she kept tossing and turning,
and kept thinking about what else she could become.
"Aha, I have it!"
cried the wife.
"I will become God."
She woke her husband and told him to run to the fish at once
and tell it her wish: she wanted to be God, being pope was not enough for her.
"Wife, wife, you have lost your mind! What are you thinking?"
"What I am thinking is my business. Go, and be quick."
Oh, dear good God, the poor fisherman shivered twice before he reached the sea.
And even more when he saw the sea!
For whatever it had been before, now the sea roared and bellowed,
it swirled and tossed as if it wanted to swallow the whole world.
The poor fisherman just stood in one place and did not even dare to open his mouth.
But the fish came, it did not wait for a question, it asked in a terrible rage:
"Is being pope not enough?
What more could she want now?"
The fisherman answered, trembling, his teeth chattering:
"Oh dear, what can I do?
Now she wants to be God!"
Oh, the enchanted prince flew into a terrible rage,
his eyes threw sparks, and he roared so loud the poor fisherman fell over in fright.
"What does the silly old goose want?
Back to the hut with her, go!"
At that very moment the sea covered everything, simply everything,
and the next morning, when it had gone back into its bed,
there was nothing on the seashore but the little hut,
and in front of it sat the fisherman and his wife, very sad, just like before.
They are still alive today, if they have not died.
